newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany paying pensions to war criminals - TV.
newsitem.headline: Germany paying pensions to war criminals - TV.

text.p: Germany has been paying supplementary "victims' pensions" worth billions of marks (dollars) each year to thousands of Nazi war criminals, a German television network said on Thursday.

The NDR television programme "Panorama" said about 50,000 war criminals and members of army units that took part in atrocities were receiving the war bonus pensions ranging from several hundred to several thousand marks each month.
The so-called "victims' pensions", which come on top of the regular pension payments, are paid to anyone who suffers from a disability linked to World War Two, or to their dependents.

The public broadcasting network, in a summary of a programme to be aired later on Thursday, said it had found one Nazi who was convicted by the German Federal Court of massacring 15 Italian women and children in 1943.
It said the man was nevertheless now collecting a 708 mark "victims' pension" each month because he was later shot in the leg while trying to escape from an Allied prison camp.

A spokesman for the German Labour Ministry, which is responsible for pensions, said the victims' pensions are paid to anyone whose health was impaired by the war. A 1950 law included a provision excluding war criminals who moved abroad.
"But there is no provision to exclude those from the victims' pensions who live in Germany because that falls under the jurisdiction of the criminal law, not social law," the spokesman said.
"If they moved abroad, they can be excluded because they are beyond the reach of German criminal law."
Gregor Gysi, the parliamentary leader of Germany's reform communist PDS party, said he was appalled by the report.

"It is monstrous that war victims' pensions are being paid to war criminals," Gysi said in a statement released in Bonn. "The government's position that they have no other option than to handle the war criminals as war victims is highly dubious."

The Panorama programme, which was due to be broadcast on Thursday evening in Germany and later on the CBS network in the United States, includes an angry denunciation of the payments by the leader of Germany's Jewish community, Ignatz Bubis.
"I could never have imagined that such people would be receiving a victims' pension," Bubis said, according to an advance press release from NDR. "It mocks the real victims."
The programme said even the widows of high-ranking Nazi leaders such as Holocaust organiser Reinhard Heydrich had received the pensions. Heydrich's wife has since died.

It also identified a concentration camp guard who was involved in atrocities but later won his claim in court that he was entitled to the pension because his kidneys were damaged during his post-war imprisonment in a drafty cell in England.
State authorities in Schleswig-Holstein tried to prevent the payments to the concentration camp guard, but had to accept the court ruling, Panorama said.

About 13 billion marks are paid each year to about 1.1 million recipients of the "victims' pensions", Panorama said. It quoted a military historian, Gerhard Schreiber, who estimated about 50,000 of those recipients are war criminals or belonged to notorious army units.

The explosive issue of pension payments to war criminals surfaced in December, when the World Jewish Council called on Germany to publish the names of former members of Hitler's Waffen SS veterans who live in Britain and the United States and receive disability pensions.

The German government refused, saying strict data protection laws prevented it from releasing such a list of names. It said, however, that any application for a pension was checked with Nazi-hunting centres and archives in Germany.
